text:
I've been looking at the promises hidden inside the word "connected".

Earlier this week I shared my team's work on mini-grid computing, green-certified offices and digital grids. Today's StoneComms post brings the same question into the classroom: what does the investment actually allow people to do?

Our researchers examined UNICEF's Africa-wide procurement for connectivity, local networks and solar power. Bundling them together makes sense. A school does not get much value from internet access when its power fails or its classroom network does not work.

For public buyers, the important price is the cost of a dependable service over time. A cheap installation can become an expensive mistake when repairs, replacement equipment and next year's bill have no budget.

For teachers and pupils, the test is more immediate: can they use it safely during the school day? Remote schools should not quietly lose out because they are harder to serve. Teachers need support, not just equipment.

I particularly like my team's insistence on five tests: reach, readiness, reliability, use and renewal. None proves that connectivity improves learning. Together, they ask whether the conditions exist for it to help.

https://stonecomms.com/research/connecting-african-schools-procurement-power-service-accountability

That is the thread through this week's work. Better investment decisions and fairer outcomes often depend on the same unglamorous details: who operates the service, who pays for it and who is responsible when it fails.

Over the coming week, we'll also be sharing existing research on two related questions. How can domestic savings finance infrastructure without pushing unsuitable risks onto pension savers? And what turns a submarine-cable landing into value for local businesses?

Follow my team at StoneComms Research & Intelligence:
https://www.linkedin.com/company/stonecomms/

For organisations facing a difficult question about African infrastructure, energy or development finance, I'd welcome a conversation about independent or commissioned research.
